questions.question: BrightCart's customers extract has customer_id 1004 appearing twice with identical values in every column. Which data quality dimension does this violate?
options: Validity
Uniqueness
Timeliness
Consistency
questions.explanation: Uniqueness means each real-world entity should appear exactly once. A duplicated customer_id row will double-count that customer in any SUM/COUNT aggregation, inflating revenue or customer-count metrics.

questions.question: A BrightCart customer row has signup_date = '2099-01-01'. Which dimension does this violate, and what does it usually signal?
options: Completeness — a missing value was defaulted incorrectly
Accuracy — an impossible real-world value, often signaling a broken upstream control like unvalidated form input
Uniqueness — the date is duplicated elsewhere
Consistency — the date format differs from other rows
questions.explanation: Accuracy asks whether a value reflects reality, not just whether it's well-formatted. A future signup date is impossible and is a Sev1-style signal: it often means a source system (e.g., a signup form) is missing date validation, which could be corrupting many other rows too.

questions.question: In the Governance Operating Model, who is typically ACCOUNTABLE for the business definition of 'customer churn,' even though they don't write the SQL?
options: The Data Custodian (platform engineer)
The Data Owner (e.g., VP of Customer Success)
The Data Steward
The BI tool vendor
questions.explanation: The Data Owner is the accountable executive who defines what the data should mean and approves access/policy. The Steward handles day-to-day quality and definitions; the Custodian implements technical controls. Confusing Owner with Custodian is a common governance failure — it makes IT accountable for business logic it can't approve.

questions.question: Two BrightCart rows encode the same segment as 'West'/'paid_search' and 'west'/'Paid_Search'. A naive GROUP BY will treat these as different segments. Which dimension is failing, and where should the fix live?
options: Validity; fix it with a one-off WHERE clause in this one query
Consistency; fix it with a normalization step (e.g., LOWER(TRIM())) in the transform layer so it doesn't recur
Timeliness; fix it by re-running the extract sooner
Completeness; fix it by deleting the row
questions.explanation: Consistency means the same fact should be represented the same way everywhere. Casing/format drift like this should be fixed centrally in the transform layer (normalize once, for every consumer), not patched ad hoc in individual queries, or it will keep resurfacing.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'data test' from 'monitoring' (data observability)?
options: They are the same thing with different names

A data test checks a known rule on a schedule (e.g., unique(customer_id)); monitoring continuously watches for unexpected shape changes (freshness, volume, schema, distribution) that nobody wrote an explicit rule for
Monitoring only applies to ML models, not data pipelines
Data tests run continuously; monitoring runs only once a year
questions.explanation: Data tests are deterministic checks against known failure modes (e.g., dbt/Great Expectations assertions). Data observability/monitoring catches the unknown failure modes — anomalies in freshness, volume, schema, or distribution that no one anticipated well enough to write an explicit rule for.

questions.question: BrightCart's orders pipeline normally finishes loading by 6 AM ET. The team commits internally to hitting that target with <0.1% row-level test failures, and separately promises stakeholders the Executive Revenue Dashboard reflects data no more than 24 hours old. Which of these is the SLO and which is the SLA?
options: The 6 AM/0.1% target is the SLA; the 24-hour promise is the SLO
The 6 AM/0.1% target is the SLO (internal engineering target); the 24-hour promise is the SLA (external commitment to stakeholders)
Both are SLAs
Both are SLOs
questions.explanation: An SLO is the internal target the data team manages against to keep its promises true. An SLA is the externally-facing commitment made to stakeholders. The SLO (pipeline completes by 6 AM, <0.1% failures) exists specifically to make the SLA (dashboard data is never more than 24 hours stale) achievable.

questions.question: An incident is detected: the `orders` table hasn't updated in 14 hours (normally hourly). Put these incident-response steps in the correct order: (1) root-cause, (2) contain, (3) postmortem, (4) detect, (5) remediate, (6) triage.
options: Detect, Triage, Contain, Root-cause, Remediate, Postmortem
Triage, Detect, Remediate, Contain, Root-cause, Postmortem
Detect, Remediate, Triage, Contain, Postmortem, Root-cause
Postmortem, Detect, Triage, Contain, Root-cause, Remediate
questions.explanation: The standard data incident workflow is: Detect (a test/observability check fires) -> Triage (assign severity, route to on-call) -> Contain (stop bad data from reaching dashboards/models) -> Root-cause (trace lineage upstream) -> Remediate (fix and backfill) -> Postmortem (blameless write-up plus a new check so it can't silently recur).

questions.question: Restricted PII data like BrightCart's customers.email should be access-controlled with which pattern?
options: Self-service — any analyst can query it immediately once they have a warehouse login
Permanent access once granted, since asking again is inefficient
Request, with a stated business reason -> Owner/Steward approval -> time-boxed grant -> periodic re-certification
No access controls are needed if the warehouse itself is encrypted
questions.explanation: Restricted data should never be self-service. The standard governance pattern is a request with a business justification, approval from the Data Owner or delegated Steward, a time-boxed grant (e.g., 90 days), and periodic re-certification (e.g., quarterly review) to revoke access that's no longer justified.
